archetype.name: Fringe Contender (defense-first, record running hot)
archetype.definition: A team whose elite pass defense and pass rush keep it in every game, but whose bottom-tier offense and negative point differential mean its 4-2 record leans on close-game wins and takeaways more than on how well it actually plays.

report.headline: A real pass defense carrying a broken offense, with a record living above it
report.take:
Denver is 4-2 and a game behind Kansas City, but it has been outscored 125-114 and its point differential implies three wins, not four. Every win has come by one score, and the Broncos are a perfect 1.000 in one-score games. That is not new. Last year's 14-3 team won .846 of its one-score games and beat its expected wins by nearly three. Sean Payton's teams have a habit of finishing close games, but a habit is not a guarantee, and the margin for error here is much thinner than it was a year ago, when the net EPA ranked 6th. This year it ranks 19th.

The defense is the reason any of this works. Against the pass it is as good as anyone: 3rd in pass EPA allowed, 4th in success rate allowed, 3rd in sacks with 18 and 3rd in QB hit rate. The takeaway count leads the league and the turnover margin is +1 a game. The last two wins were built almost entirely on it, with five sacks and three takeaways in each. The run defense is a different story. It ranks 26th in rush EPA allowed and 28th in explosive run rate, and the tackling is the worst in the league by missed-tackle rate. Kansas City ran for 220 yards in the opener, and that soft middle is the defense's real weak point.

The offense is the problem, and nothing in the numbers hides it. Denver is 31st in yards per game, 28th in success rate and 24th in EPA. Bo Nix threw for 123 and 107 yards in the last two games. The line keeps him clean on contact (1st in QB hit rate allowed, 6th in sack rate), but it gives up pressure at the 26th-ranked rate and creates almost nothing before contact in the run game (25th). J.K. Dobbins carries most of the load behind it. Payton has not gone for it on fourth down once this season. Taken together, this is an offense designed not to lose games, and so far the defense has made that enough.

The path forward depends on whether the takeaways and the close-game finishes hold up, because the offense is not about to start winning shootouts. The defense is good enough to keep Denver in the wild-card race all year. But Surtain and Hufanga are both out this week, Kansas City comes to town next, and Buffalo and Pittsburgh are still ahead, so that record will get tested.

strengths.title: Elite pass defense and pass rush
strengths.body: Denver smothers quarterbacks: top-three in pass EPA allowed, sacks and QB hit rate, with a top-four success rate allowed. It rests on a pass rush that wins without needing to blitz everyone, and it fits the 2024-25 pattern of a top-ten defense, so it is the most durable thing about this team. The caveat is that two of its best defensive backs are currently out.

strengths.title: Winning the turnover battle
strengths.body: The league-leading takeaway total and a +1 turnover margin per game have decided games: the defense took the ball away three times in each of the last two wins. Pressure produces some of those turnovers, so part of it is real. The pace of takeaways usually cools, though, and the offense has no cushion if it does.

strengths.title: Clean pocket on contact
strengths.body: Nix is almost never hit (1st in QB hit rate allowed) and rarely sacked (6th in sack rate). That keeps drives from going backward and protects the turnover margin. It is a real line strength, even if the pressure numbers are worse.

concerns.title: An offense that can't move the ball
concerns.body: The offense ranks 31st in yards per game, 28th in success rate and 26th in scoring. The passing game has shrunk to barely 100 yards in each of the last two weeks. Behind a run game that creates little before contact, this looks structural rather than a slump, and it is the main reason the point differential is negative.

concerns.title: Record propped up by close games
concerns.body: Denver has won every one-score game it has played, and its point differential implies three wins, not four. It ran the same way last year, which suggests some of it is coaching and situational skill. A perfect mark still tends to come back toward the middle, and with this offense most games will stay close.

concerns.title: Soft, poor-tackling run defense
concerns.body: The defense ranks 26th in rush EPA allowed and 28th in explosive run rate, and it has the worst missed-tackle rate in the league. Teams that can lean on the run, as Kansas City did in Week 1, can stay out of reach of the pass rush. This is a real flaw, not a product of game script.

trend.note: The record has gone the right way, with three straight wins including an upset of Seattle. Underneath it, the passing game has faded to its weakest output of the year while the defense has taken over, with five sacks and three takeaways in each of the last two games. That is a narrow way to keep winning.

nextGame.headline: A leaky Arizona secondary is exactly what this offense needs
nextGame.body:
Denver goes to Arizona as a 4.5-point favorite (moneyline -230, total 43.5) after ten days of rest following its Thursday win. Arizona is 2-4 with the 30th-ranked point differential, and its defense is the weak side of the matchup. It ranks 30th in pass EPA allowed, 30th against deep passes and 29th in explosive passes allowed, and it ranks last in EPA allowed to opposing WR1s. For a Denver offense that has struggled to throw, this is the softest secondary it has faced. Arizona's run defense (11th in rush EPA allowed) is sturdier, so the yards are more likely to come through the air than on the ground. On the other side, Jacoby Brissett runs a middling offense (18th in EPA) that controls the clock well, 5th in time of possession.

Availability matters on both sides. Denver will be without Pat Surtain II and Talanoa Hufanga, both listed out, which takes a top corner and an every-down safety out of the league's 3rd-ranked pass defense. Pat Bryant is on IR, so Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton will carry even more of the passing game. Arizona is short in the backfield and at safety: Jeremiyah Love is out and James Conner remains on IR, while safeties Andrew Wingard and Wydett Williams Jr. are both out. That leaves an already leaky back end thinner still, and it blunts a run game that could otherwise test Denver's weakest unit.

waysToWin.title: Take shots at Arizona's depleted safeties
waysToWin.body: Arizona gives up big plays through the air and is missing two safeties. If Nix gets Waddle and Sutton the ball downfield early, Denver can post its first comfortable lead in weeks. This is the clearest mismatch on the field.

waysToWin.title: Make Arizona's offense one-dimensional
waysToWin.body: With Love out and Conner on IR, Arizona's ability to attack Denver's poor run defense shrinks. If Brissett has to throw on long downs, Denver's pass rush, top three in sacks and hits, can produce the kind of drive-killing takeaways that won the last two games.

waysToWin.title: Throw from a clean pocket
waysToWin.body: Arizona's pass rush ranks 25th in pressure rate. Denver's protection, already the best in the league at keeping Nix from being hit, should give him time to work through reads, which has not always been true this year.

waysToLose.title: The secondary sags without Surtain, Hufanga
waysToLose.body: Losing an 86%-snap corner and a 93%-snap safety at once is a real hit, and Denver already ranks 27th in EPA allowed to tight ends. If Arizona works the middle and the sideline Surtain would have covered, the pass defense that carries this team could look ordinary.

waysToLose.title: The offense stalls again
waysToLose.body: If Nix can't take advantage of the soft coverage, Denver's 28th-ranked success rate and Arizona's ability to hold the ball turn this into a short game with few possessions. That is exactly the kind of game a 4.5-point underdog can steal.

waysToLose.title: Missed tackles turn into chunk runs
waysToLose.body: Even with backup backs, Arizona runs successfully at a 12th-ranked rate, and Denver misses more tackles than anyone. A few broken runs would let Arizona sustain drives and keep the pass rush off the field.

nextGame.watch: Whether Nix pushes the ball deep to Waddle against an Arizona secondary missing both of its safeties. If the passing game can't get going in this matchup, it may not get going this season.

restOfSeason.body:
The pass defense and pass rush are real and should keep Denver a tough out all year, especially once Surtain and Hufanga return. The offense is the limiting factor. Its yardage and success rates point to an attack that will hover near 19-20 points a game unless the passing game finds something. Two things will likely cool: the perfect record in one-score games and the league-leading takeaway pace. Either one going away costs wins this offense can't easily replace.

The schedule cuts both ways. Miami and the Chargers twice look like wins, and Las Vegas twice and the Jets are winnable. Kansas City next week, Buffalo and a road trip to Pittsburgh are the tests of whether this is a playoff team or a winning record waiting to come back down. Expect a team in the wild-card hunt, around nine or ten wins, that wins ugly and loses whenever it falls behind by more than a score.
swingFactors: Whether the passing game revives behind Waddle and Sutton
How quickly Surtain and Hufanga return
Whether the close-game and takeaway luck holds

confidence.note: Six games is a small sample, but the profile is consistent. A defense this good, an offense this limited and the reliance on close-game results all match the past two seasons.
